title: The Tithe Bridge
special_element: **The bridge reads what each person values most, and will not let them pass until they set it down on the stones — and mean it.** Not forever. The item waits on the span, exactly where they left it, in plain sight the whole crossing; they may take it up again on the far side. But they have to let go of it for true, or the bridge knows. A warrior's father's sword. A merchant's last letter from someone dead. A child's luck-stone carried since before they could read. The bridge has no patience for decoys — it returns them, gently, to your feet.
summary: The bridge is narrow — one cart's width, no more — its stones worn smooth as old soap by ten thousand crossings.
body: The bridge is narrow — one cart's width, no more — its stones worn smooth as old soap by ten thousand crossings. The mortar between them is the colour of dried blood, and every parapet stone is carved with an open hand, palm up, waiting. Step onto the span and the whole structure *settles*: a low groan that runs abutment to abutment, stone talking to stone. Something has noticed you.
The Tithe Bridge has stood at this ford longer than the village behind you has had a name. Most travellers cross without incident. The bridge is not always hungry.

When it is, the carved hands are the tell. Locals call it *taking its due* — flat, matter-of-fact, the way they'd describe a tax. Outsiders call it a curse. The bridge does not care what it is called.

It does not want coin. The bandits camped at the near bank want coin — they hold the near bank and demand a toll of their own; the bridge is indifferent to theirs. The bridge wants something older. (This is a sacrifice-puzzle, not a haunting — for the bridge with a living thing beneath it, see *Under the Bridge*.)
Decide before play whether the bridge is live for this crossing. At easy difficulty, deploy it once — as a character moment, not a resource drain.
The reveal lands hardest when the *player* names what their character values — don't assign it, ask. *"What does [name] put down?"* Then give them a beat. The crossing is theirs, not yours.
If the party has already dealt with the bandits on the near bank, their refusal to cross becomes a clue they can now read: the boast about holding this ford rings false in a useful way.

Special element: **The bridge reads what each person values most, and will not let them pass until they set it down on the stones — and mean it.** Not forever. The item waits on the span, exactly where they left it, in plain sight the whole crossing; they may take it up again on the far side. But they have to let go of it for true, or the bridge knows. A warrior's father's sword. A merchant's last letter from someone dead. A child's luck-stone carried since before they could read. The bridge has no patience for decoys — it returns them, gently, to your feet.
trigger: The bridge is hungry only on a crossing the DM marks *live* — not every time. Signs it is live: the carved hands are warm to the touch, and the groan as you step onto the span runs longer than stone should make.
clues: The parapet carvings: open hands, palms up. Not threatening. Waiting.
Old offerings wedged in the stonework: a child's boot, a split arrowshaft, a plain ring with no inscription.
Any local, asked directly: *"It takes its due, when it's of a mind to. You'll know."*
The bandits at the near bank have not crossed in three weeks. They value their lives too much to mean it.
solution: Each character sets the object they value most on the stones, crosses, and takes it up on the far bank.
The test is sincerity, not loss. A character who genuinely values nothing they carry crosses freely — the bridge goes quiet under their feet.
consequences: **Comply:** the stones hold firm; the objects wait untouched, exactly where they were set.
**Refuse:** the stones shift — not enough to kill, enough to unsteady. The crossing is possible but lurching; fumble a check and something goes into the gorge anyway.
**Deceive:** the decoy comes back to your feet. The bridge waits. It has waited longer than you.
**Force it:** the bridge is old, and feels no pain, and has survived worse. Nothing happens to the bridge.

title: The Ledger Door
special_element: A true name opens the door — but the ledger keeps it. When a PC writes their name and the door swings, have them turn back, once they are through, and look at the page. Their name is already there, crossed out — in an older hand, in ink dry long before they stepped up to write. Somewhere in this ledger they were always here. And someone had already marked them as not coming back.
summary: Category: Puzzle · Tier: 1 · Difficulty: medium · Biome: ruins · Mood: mysterious
body: Category: Puzzle · Tier: 1 · Difficulty: medium · Biome: ruins · Mood: mysterious

The door has no handle, no keyhole, no hinge — pale stone set flush with the wall, seamless but for a brass bracket at chest height holding an open ledger. The pages are brown at the edges, the ink the colour of dried blood. The air is close and still, thick with old paper and, under it, something sharper: char, as though pages burned here an hour ago.

The ledger is the lock. Write a name and the door answers — but only to a true name. Aliases, titles, pet names, invented ones scorch off the moment the ink dries, leaving the paper clean. Only a name the writer truly answers to — a birth name, the name at the back of their own mind — holds. When it does, the door grinds inward on a breath of cold air.
The ledger is not blank. Every page within reach is full: names in a dozen hands across what looks like centuries. Most are legible. A few are struck through with one hard stroke.

If your table has met the self-updating roster at the Hollow Ward Post, the difference is the whole point: that ledger writes down who passes through, after the fact. This one was filled before anyone arrived. It does not record the living — it waits for them.

Special element: A true name opens the door — but the ledger keeps it. When a PC writes their name and the door swings, have them turn back, once they are through, and look at the page. Their name is already there, crossed out — in an older hand, in ink dry long before they stepped up to write. Somewhere in this ledger they were always here. And someone had already marked them as not coming back.
consequences: A character who reads old scripts can scan earlier pages: most are single names, no dates. A handful carry a margin mark — a circle with a line through it — and those names are also struck through.
The table beneath the bracket is scorched in repeated smears. Someone tried false names here, many times, and the charring runs deep.

A PC who studies the crossed-out names and beats a DC 12 Investigation or History check recognises one: a minor historical figure who vanished exploring these ruins. No record of their death was ever found.
The crossed-out name is the slow burn. It blocks nothing, but it is now a fact in the world. Who made the mark, and when? The answer may be sessions away.

Decide before play: does the circle-and-line carry mechanical weight — a curse, a pact, something that tracks the bearer — or is it simply a mark the door makes, its meaning dead with whoever built it? Either works; the second is harder to resolve and lingers longer.

title: The Drowning Stair
special_element: The ward is not listening to the words. It is listening to the pitch. Speak the right answer in the wrong register and the water still rises a step. Sing the *wrong* answer on the right note and the party earns a pause — one round in which the water holds and the ward's tone repeats, as if offering another chance. The puzzle is half riddle, half performance: knowing the answer is not enough. You have to be willing to sing it back.
summary: Category: Puzzle · Tier: 2 · Difficulty: hard · Biome: underwater · Mood: grim
body: Category: Puzzle · Tier: 2 · Difficulty: hard · Biome: underwater · Mood: grim

The stairwell drops in a straight column through black water, twelve steps just visible below the surface. Each one glows faintly — not with light but with the absence of silt, scrubbed clean by something old and patient. And from below, rising through the water and into your chest rather than your ears, comes a low repeating note. Not a sound. A pressure. A question, waiting to be asked.

The Drowning Stair links two submerged chambers across a vertical drop of roughly thirty feet. Whoever held this place sealed it not with a lock but with a voice-ward — a riddle sung into the stone at the building, set to play on repeat until it is answered.

The stair is half-dry at first. The bottom six steps are underwater; the top six are not. Every wrong answer — spoken, signed, or held up on a slate against the water — raises the level by one step. A right answer clears nothing on its own; the ward is not done with the party until it hears what it wants, the way it wants to hear it.

The riddle concerns carrying something without holding it: grief, knowledge, a name. The wording drifts each time it cycles; the logic does not. The answer is not unique — the ward accepts anything that fits.

When all twelve steps go under, the stair locks. The door at the column's base seals with a sound like an exhaled breath and will not reopen from this side. The water holds, still and permanent. The only way out is back up through the entry chamber — if anyone can still reach it.

**Before play, decide:** is there a strict correct answer, or does any sincere sung response on the right pitch count? The first rewards lateral thinking; the second rewards roleplay nerve, and plays better for groups who find riddles punishing.

**The ward's pitch** is a low chest note, near the bottom of a human singing range. Matching it is a DC 13 Charisma (Performance) check. On a natural 1 the attempt is far enough off that the water rises an extra step — the ward takes it for mockery.

**Reveal timing:** don't announce the singing mechanic. Let one or two wrong spoken answers raise the water first. When a player hums the answer, or sings it half as a joke, hold the water still a beat longer than it should be — and let them notice.

**If the party is drowning:** a previous visitor hangs in the water near the foot of the stair. They did not make it. A scrap of vellum is stiff in one hand. If retrieved, it shows the riddle, a possible answer, and one line crammed at the bottom in a hurried hand — *sing it.*
**At the table:** hum the note yourself. One sustained low note from the DM, held for two seconds before you describe the ward, changes the whole room. The players will not forget the session.

Special element: The ward is not listening to the words. It is listening to the pitch. Speak the right answer in the wrong register and the water still rises a step. Sing the *wrong* answer on the right note and the party earns a pause — one round in which the water holds and the ward's tone repeats, as if offering another chance. The puzzle is half riddle, half performance: knowing the answer is not enough. You have to be willing to sing it back.

title: Salt-Sheet Riddle
special_element: The solution is not a cipher. It is silence. The party must read with their eyes only — no dictation, no reading aloud to share. The lock is habit, and the discipline is social: can this group agree to stay quiet long enough to recover what they came for? It lands harder once they know the lore: the salt *is* the scholars. To speak their words aloud is to take those words from them for good. Silence is not a workaround. It is the correct way to treat the dead.
summary: Category: Puzzle · Tier: 3 · Difficulty: medium · Biome: ruins · Mood: melancholy
body: Category: Puzzle · Tier: 3 · Difficulty: medium · Biome: ruins · Mood: melancholy

The page is the size of a large hand, pale as old bone, and it catches the lantern-light like something still wet. There is no ink — the words are pressed into the salt itself, raised letters fine as veins. Lean close and it smells of iron, and under that, something older than paper: a library-smell, in a place where no library has stood for a very long time.

Salt-sheet riddles arise whenever the party tries to read the surviving fragments of the Library of Salt. The sheets are not ciphered. They are not warded. A scholar could read one in minutes — if scholars worked in silence.

The letter-surface is crystalline, and vibration shatters the raised matrix. A shouted word destroys a sheet in seconds; a careful recitation strips three or four minutes off its legible life. Most parties learn this by accident: someone reads the first line aloud and watches a row of letters soften, hiss, and fall away as fine powder.
The puzzle is recognising what just happened before the page is gone.

Decide before play: **which sheet carries the critical information**, and whether partial recovery still moves the plot or creates a genuine dead end. If a wall would be too punishing, let a half-destroyed sheet hold the key piece with enough gaps to make it ambiguous rather than a hard block.

The texture is grief, not danger. When letters are lost, describe what they were: a name, a number, a sentence that was nearly a conclusion. Players who carry "The Salt That Was Words" lore into this scene already know what they are destroying — and the silence will feel like respect, not a mechanic.
If they come in ignorant, this is where it lands. Let them ask, afterwards, what the salt was. Then tell them.

Special element: The solution is not a cipher. It is silence. The party must read with their eyes only — no dictation, no reading aloud to share. The lock is habit, and the discipline is social: can this group agree to stay quiet long enough to recover what they came for? It lands harder once they know the lore: the salt *is* the scholars. To speak their words aloud is to take those words from them for good. Silence is not a workaround. It is the correct way to treat the dead.
clues: **Cause and effect:** The first letter lost is always the first letter spoken. Observable, if anyone is watching.
**Margin note:** One fragment carries barely-legible salt-text along its lower edge — *"breath unmakes us."* A character reading silently who passes DC 13 Investigation finds it.

**The shape of the damage:** On worn fragments, the letters at the far edges are crisper than those at the centre — as if someone once leaned over and whispered onto the page. The edges survived because no one breathed on them.
**The sound:** In total silence, dissolving letters make a noise like fine sand dragged across glass. It is not a warning. It is the sound of loss, and it is small.
solution: Read without speaking. Characters who communicate by writing, gesture, or sign while in the Library — and who pass DC 14 Intelligence (History or Arcana) reading silently — recover a sheet's full contents intact.

Magical methods that move no air (telepathy, *Sending*, *Message* whispered below the threshold of resonance) are DM's call. Baseline: if it doesn't move air across the page, it doesn't shatter the surface.
consequences: **Success:** The sheet yields its contents whole. A disciplined party can recover several fragments in a session. Each intact reading leaves them holding someone's last thoughts — a fact that may matter to NPCs of salt-lineage or to threads rooted in the Library.
**Partial:** The DM chooses which section survives — the beginning, the end, or the crucial middle. A crumbling sheet gives enough to raise questions, not enough to answer them cleanly.
**Failure:** The page is gone. The hiss is brief. Whatever it held is held by no one now. No undo, no reconstruction — nothing left but the weight of it.

title: The Mirror Vote
special_element: The mirror is not a lie detector — but the room is built to make everyone assume it is, and that assumption is the trap. What it actually measures is whether every reflection moves in *perfect unison* as the sentence is spoken, which happens only when everyone believes the same thing at the moment they say it. A rehearsed lie the whole party has come to believe passes cleanly. A technically true statement, spoken by five voices where even one privately doubts it, splinters the reflections out of sync — and the mirror reads that flicker as failure.
summary: Category: Puzzle · Region: none · Tier: 2 · Difficulty: hard · Biome: planar · Mood: mysterious
body: Category: Puzzle · Region: none · Tier: 2 · Difficulty: hard · Biome: planar · Mood: mysterious

The chamber is round and walled floor to ceiling in black glass, polished so bright that every torch becomes six. It is silent in a way that swallows footsteps — no echo, no draft, not even the scrape of a boot sounds twice. And the reflections are a half-beat slow: raise a hand, and the mirrored hand rises after you, as if the room is thinking it over first.

At the chamber's center stands a plinth of the same black glass, and set into it, a single unblinking eye of mirror the size of a shield. It asks one question, once, of the whole party at once: *"Speak, together, the true value of the thing you seek."*
It will not repeat itself. It will not clarify. The party has one attempt to answer as a group — a single sentence, spoken in unison — and the mirror judges the instant the last word lands.

Accept, and the plinth splits open and the way forward is clear. Reject, and every mirrored surface flexes inward at once, and the six-fold reflections stop moving like people: they step out of the glass to make the party's failure permanent.

**Trigger:** the party reads the question aloud, or a scout steps within arm's reach of the plinth. Either way the whole party present is bound to answer — there is no opting out once it has spoken. **Clues:** earlier rooms (or an NPC who faced the mirror and lived) should plant the idea that this is a truth test — that's the intended misdirect. The subtler tell, easy to miss on a first pass: the reflections only lag when one person watches, and fall into lockstep when the whole party looks at once. The mirror cares about the group, not the individual. **Solution:** the party agrees out loud before answering — one sentence, one shared conviction, spoken together. A true statement works if everyone believes it; a false one works if everyone has talked themselves into it. What fails is disagreement dressed as agreement — five people saying the same words while believing five different things. **Consequences:** success splits the plinth and opens the way on. Failure sends the reflections out of the glass — treat as a swarm of Mirror-forms (use a shadow's stat block, minus the Strength-drain trait; swap in a **Discord Lash**: on a hit, the target must repeat its last spoken sentence before it may act) that fight until the party retreats from the chamber, at which point the mirror resets and may be tried again.

Special element: The mirror is not a lie detector — but the room is built to make everyone assume it is, and that assumption is the trap. What it actually measures is whether every reflection moves in *perfect unison* as the sentence is spoken, which happens only when everyone believes the same thing at the moment they say it. A rehearsed lie the whole party has come to believe passes cleanly. A technically true statement, spoken by five voices where even one privately doubts it, splinters the reflections out of sync — and the mirror reads that flicker as failure.

title: Frostbite Cipher
special_element: The cipher yields only to living breath, only a few symbols at a time, and only once per patch before the ice refreezes clean — no lantern, spell, or flame reads it faster. Solving it is an act of memory and patience, not clever tools.
summary: Category: Puzzle · Tier: 3 · Difficulty: medium · Biome: frozen · Mood: mysterious
body: Category: Puzzle · Tier: 3 · Difficulty: medium · Biome: frozen · Mood: mysterious

A vault door of black iron, sealed under a skin of clear ice thick as a fist. Beneath the ice, scratched into the metal, run rows of marks — yet the surface above them is smooth, blank, unreadable. The cold pouring off it bites at any bare skin, and it smells faintly of old smoke, as though a fire burned here long before the ice ever came.

The smith who warded this door distrusted eyes as much as thieves. The cipher is cut so shallow that it hides from both sight and fingertip — the only thing that draws it out is a thin fog of condensation.

Breathe on the metal and hold it a few seconds: the fog beads, then fades, and in the half-second before it vanishes the etched lines darken against the frost — one word or symbol at a time, never the whole cipher at once. Bring a torch close and the opposite happens: the surface ice melts and erases whatever mark was about to surface.
Anyone working the door has to keep returning to breathe on fresh patches, piece by piece, memory carrying what the ice refuses to hold still long enough to show twice.

Special element: The cipher yields only to living breath, only a few symbols at a time, and only once per patch before the ice refreezes clean — no lantern, spell, or flame reads it faster. Solving it is an act of memory and patience, not clever tools.
consequences: **Trigger:** any character breathes on the door, or is told to by another who's read this text.

**Clues:** each breath reveals 3–5 symbols in one spot; the full cipher runs roughly thirty symbols, scattered across the door's face, and never repeats a location twice in a session unless the party rests and returns.

**Solution:** the party must reconstruct the full phrase from partial reveals — encourage note-taking, a sketched map of the door, or an Intelligence check (DC 15) to recall a missed section instead of re-breathing it.

**Consequences:** a correct phrase spoken aloud (not written) unseals the door. A wrong phrase drops the temperature around it low enough to threaten frostbite — treat as a failed Constitution save or a level of exhaustion, DM's call. Decide before play whether repeated failures eventually shatter the ice and destroy the cipher for good, locking the vault permanently.

title: The Red Waterwheel
special_element: Brake the wheel while the black spoke sits at the top of its turn and the burned town comes back for up to an hour. Wedge it, rope it or hold it by hand. The ash thins, the foundations rise into timber and thatch, and the town's last night plays out around the party, clear as breath on glass. Its people go about their business with no idea anyone is watching. The party can see what happened: the fire was no accident. Soldiers carrying torches bar the doors from the outside, house by house. Only one door is left unbarred, the inn's. Let go of the wheel, or let the hour run out, and everything snaps back to ash, rubble and silence. Then the wheel goes on ticking as if nothing happened.
summary: Category: Puzzle · Region: Callow's Ford · Tier: 1 · Difficulty: medium · Biome: frontier · Mood: mysterious
body: Category: Puzzle · Region: Callow's Ford · Tier: 1 · Difficulty: medium · Biome: frontier · Mood: mysterious

At the river's dead bend stands a mill wheel painted the red of old barns, and it turns. There is no water under it, only ash and the broken teeth of a foundation. Still the wheel groans forward a hand's width at a time, slow and steady, like something counting. Lay your palm flat on a spoke and you feel it: no push of a current, just a tick, a tick, a tick, patient as a clock that has never once stopped.

The wheel drove Callow's Ford's mill before the fire. It is one of the few pieces of the old town still standing above the ash line, and it has not touched water in fifty years. It turns anyway: twelve spokes, one spoke every hour, each step landing on the chime of the garrison bell that still rings across the rubble. The few locals who have noticed call it bad luck and walk wide around it.
One spoke is darker than weather can explain. The black is not soot on the surface. It is a scorch burned deep into the grain.

Decide before play how much more the vision shows beyond the barred doors. A gentle version keeps the party at a distance, with smoke and torchlight. A sharp version puts them close enough to the fire to hear the voices of the people inside. Either way the party leaves knowing the town was burned on purpose. They don't know why, or why one door was spared. That knowledge pays off on its own: it changes how they look at the garrison bell, the innkeeper who "never could say", and anyone in town who is old enough to remember. The puzzle stands alone and rewards curiosity, careful timing and a hard choice about who stays behind at the wheel, whether or not the party ever chases the question.

Special element: Brake the wheel while the black spoke sits at the top of its turn and the burned town comes back for up to an hour. Wedge it, rope it or hold it by hand. The ash thins, the foundations rise into timber and thatch, and the town's last night plays out around the party, clear as breath on glass. Its people go about their business with no idea anyone is watching. The party can see what happened: the fire was no accident. Soldiers carrying torches bar the doors from the outside, house by house. Only one door is left unbarred, the inn's. Let go of the wheel, or let the hour run out, and everything snaps back to ash, rubble and silence. Then the wheel goes on ticking as if nothing happened.
trigger: **Trigger:** anyone who keeps a hand on the wheel for a full minute notices the ticking rhythm. They can try to match it to the garrison bell.
**Clue 1:** the wheel has twelve spokes, and the bell rings the hours. Let an observant PC connect the count without a roll.
**Clue 2:** the black spoke doesn't match the weathering on the other eleven. It reads as burned, not aged.

**Clue 3:** the one unburned inn in Callow's Ford keeps its lamp lit all night. Asked why, the innkeeper says they "never could say." The lamp faces the wheel, and it is the only light that also burns in the vision.
solution: Stop the wheel with the black spoke at the top. A crowbar, a spear haft or two strong backs pushing against the turn all work. No roll is needed to set the brake. The wheel keeps pushing against it, though, and one PC has to stay at the wheel to hold it. That PC sees the vision only from the dead bend, as a glow on the ash. Every ten minutes the holder makes a Strength check (DC 12, swappable). On a failure the brake slips and the vision ends at once. A second PC can help (advantage), but that means another person who doesn't go into the town.
consequences: While the vision holds, the party can walk through the town, but nothing in it can see or hear them. The barred doors, the soldiers and the unbarred inn are always there. Add anything else they witness yourself: a bell rung out of turn, an officer's shout, faces at a shuttered window. Each sight should raise the question of why, never answer it. The town is laid out as it was, not as it is now. Anyone standing on a vision floor that doesn't exist anymore when the vision collapses drops into the burned cellar beneath (1d6 bludgeoning, DC 12 Dexterity save for half) and has to climb out of the rubble. The deeper the party goes, the more they see, and the more solid ground they give up. The black spoke comes back to the top every twelve hours, but the wheel won't take a brake again until it has ticked a full day.

title: The Avalanche Lock
special_element: **The lock is read by the load, not by the carvings.** The notches look like a numbered order, and they lie. They record the order in which the builders would pull the wedges to *release* the dam on purpose. That is exactly the wrong order for freeing a single cart. The true order is found by ear and by hand: pull the quietest wedge first and the loudest last. Every pull changes which wedges are singing. The reveal: if the party follows the carved order faithfully, the whole slope comes down. The founders left it as a last resort, a way to drop the drift on the valley if it was ever overrun.
summary: Category: Puzzle · Tier: 2 · Difficulty: medium · Biome: frozen · Mood: grim
body: Category: Puzzle · Tier: 2 · Difficulty: medium · Biome: frozen · Mood: grim

Above the village roofs, a wall of snow as tall as a barn hangs in the gully, and it creaks. Rows of black timber wedges, each as thick as a man's thigh, are driven into the packed drift. Every wedge is rimed with frost and carved with worn notches. A laden cart is jammed against the dam's upper lip, its canvas frozen stiff as board, one wheel turning slowly over nothing. The air bites the back of your throat. Far below, chimney smoke rises straight and thin, and a dog barks at the slope as though it can hear it breathing.
Generations ago, the villagers built the Avalanche Lock into the snow-choked throat of the gully above their homes. The wedges pin a hanging drift in place so it can never slide as one mass.

Someone drove a cart onto the dam in the dark, and it is stuck fast on the upper lip. The wedges are all that stands between the slope and the roofs. Freeing the cart means touching them. Nothing has fallen yet. This is the hour before the slide, while it can still be stopped, not the dig afterward.

There are nine wedges in three rows of three. Each carries one, two, or three cuts plus a small sign: a hearth, a fir, or a crow. The wedges don't share the load evenly. Pull the wrong one and its weight shifts onto the neighbours, which groan and spit ice.
Let the party learn this by looking and listening rather than through explanation. A straining wedge sounds higher and drips meltwater. A slack wedge rocks under a hand.

Use a clock of **6 Strain**. Each wrong pull adds 1 Strain. A tense, noisy delay adds 1 on a failed check. At 3 Strain, a crack runs across the drift and snow hisses down onto the lower rooftops. At 6, the slope goes.

**Observe (Wisdom (Survival), DC 13):** shows which wedge carries the least load. After three correct pulls in a row, the party gets the next read free. **Pull a wedge:** a Strength check (DC 12), or a rope-and-team effort that needs no check. Brute force works but adds 1 Strain. **Read the carvings (Intelligence (Investigation), DC 14):** shows that the notches follow a release pattern and are a warning, not a guide. A party that works this out before pulling avoids the trap entirely. **Brace the load:** a character who wedges a spar or shield against a loud wedge buys one pull without Strain, but stands in the drift's path while doing it. **Villagers:** fetching help from below costs time (+1 Strain), but the villagers bring ropes and the lock's history. A local can offer: *"The quiet ones first, the old ones always said."*

**Introduce:** let the party hear the dam before they see it: a low groan under the wind, then a wedge cracking like a knuckle. **Voice it:** give each wedge its own note, such as a tin whine, a wet creak, or a dead silence. Use your voice to make the players listen. **The lever:** the cart is not the stakes; the roofs are. Keep the village in sight and in earshot. **The reveal:** spring the carved-order trap the moment a player says "just follow the numbers." **Pairing:** The Buried Caravan is the rescue after the snow has fallen. This is the hour before, when careful hands can still keep it up. **Dialogue seed:** *"My gran said the lock was made to hold the mountain, and made to drop it. Nobody ever told her which was the joke."*

Special element: **The lock is read by the load, not by the carvings.** The notches look like a numbered order, and they lie. They record the order in which the builders would pull the wedges to *release* the dam on purpose. That is exactly the wrong order for freeing a single cart. The true order is found by ear and by hand: pull the quietest wedge first and the loudest last. Every pull changes which wedges are singing. The reveal: if the party follows the carved order faithfully, the whole slope comes down. The founders left it as a last resort, a way to drop the drift on the valley if it was ever overrun.
resolution: **Clean:** the cart rolls free and every wedge is driven back home. The village keeps its lock and its founders' secret.
**Partial:** the cart comes free, but a slab breaks away and buries outbuildings or the top road. No one dies, and the village remembers who was on the dam.
**Failure:** the slide hits the lower roofs. Decide before play whether anyone is caught in it, and make sure the party hears it happen.
scaling: **Tier 2 baseline** as written. For a party of 2–3, drop the clock to 5 Strain and let a single Strength check pull any wedge. For 6 or more, add a smaller second lock of four wedges above the first, with its own 3-Strain clock. Both locks must be worked. If the upper clock fills, its slab slides onto the main dam and adds 2 Strain there.
**Lower tier:** remove the false carvings and keep only the listening puzzle.
**Higher tier:** put a living creature in the cart. Its cries make the wedges ring and drown out their notes.
rewards: **The cart's cargo:** an iron-bound crate of winter stores bound for the village, plus a few coins.
**The village's trust:** a hearth, a bed, and a favour to call in later.
**The founders' secret:** the release order, now understood. With it, the party could drop this drift on purpose if the valley is ever overrun.
